blocks.text: Move data between domain objects and storage with a separate mapper, so neither side knows about the other.

A **data mapper** translates between rich domain objects and the storage shape: rows, documents, columns with other names. The domain class has no `save` and no SQL. Storage has no business rules. Both can evolve independently, which is the whole value.

items: **Domain side:** invariants, value objects, behavior, no persistence code.
**Mapper:** the only code that knows both shapes.

blocks.text: JPA/Hibernate is a metadata-driven data mapper: annotations or XML describe the mapping and the `EntityManager` executes it. The annotations are the entity's one concession to persistence.

walkthrough.note: A domain object with an invariant-checking value object. It imports nothing about storage and has no `save`.
The storage shape: a flat record whose field `emailAddr` differs from the domain's `Email` type, standing in for a table row.
The mapper owns both directions. `find` hydrates a `Customer`; `save` flattens it to a `Row`. Private methods keep conversions in one place.
The domain object is loaded, changed through its own behavior and handed back to the mapper. It never sees the table.
Hydration goes through the domain constructors, so a corrupt row fails loudly instead of creating an invalid object.

blocks.text: Clean domain model over a legacy billing table.

A twenty-year-old table has columns like `CUST_NM`, `STAT_CD` ('A', 'S', 'C') and a split address. The new domain wants a `Customer` with a `Status` enum and an `Address` value object. A mapper converts codes to enums and merges columns into value objects. When the schema is later refactored, only the mapper changes. MyBatis result maps do the same declaratively.

lines: return new Customer(r.id(), r.custNm(), status, addr);

blocks.text: Payoff: the legacy schema leaks nowhere into business code, and the table can be migrated without touching the domain.

lists.title: Use when
items: The domain model is rich and shaped differently from the schema.
Domain logic must be testable without a database.
Schema and model evolve at different speeds.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Classes and tables are nearly identical and logic is thin; the mapper is pure overhead.
A small team needs rapid CRUD (see Active Record).

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Hand-written mappers drifting out of sync with the schema; cover them with round-trip tests.
Lazy loading hidden in the mapper causing N+1 queries.
Mapping that bypasses constructors and builds invalid objects.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: Hand-rolled mapper for a model an ORM could map in minutes.
A mapper per class that merely copies identically named fields.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records and compact constructors keep hydration validated; MapStruct can generate repetitive conversions.
Records make good storage rows and DTO shapes, with the mapper converting to richer domain classes.

rows.difference: Active Record puts persistence in the entity, coupling it to the row. A data mapper keeps the entity ignorant, at the price of an extra layer.
A mapper's API is persistence-shaped: insert, update, delete, find by column. A repository wraps mappers in a collection-like, domain-worded interface per aggregate.
The unit of work tracks which objects changed; mappers perform the writes for those objects at commit.
A DTO carries data across a boundary and has no behavior. A mapper converts between shapes and may build behavior-rich domain objects.

entries.name: EntityManager
entries.detail: Entity mappings translate classes to tables; entities need no save method and no base class.

entries.name: Mapper interfaces and result maps
entries.detail: Explicit SQL plus mapping rules turn result sets into plain objects.

entries.name: Aggregate mapping
entries.detail: Maps aggregate roots to tables without a persistence context or lazy loading.

entries.detail: Pluggable conversions between fetched `Record`s and plain objects in each direction; `fetchInto(Class)` uses the default mapper.

exercises.scenario: A domain model uses value objects, enums and no setters. The legacy table has cryptic columns and denormalized fields, and the schema will be refactored separately next quarter. The model should not change when it does.

options.why: A mapper isolates both shapes so schema changes touch only the mapping.
Entities would mirror the table's shape and carry persistence, so schema changes ripple into the model.
A DTO carries data over a boundary but does not translate to and from storage.
A repository defines the access API but still needs a translation mechanism inside.

exercises.prompt: Explain Data Mapper in your own words: who knows what, and how does it differ from Active Record?

modelAnswer.text: A data mapper is a layer that converts between domain objects and storage shapes in both directions. The domain object knows nothing about persistence and storage knows nothing about behavior. Active Record instead lets the entity load and save itself, which is simpler but couples the class to its table.

keyPoints: Active Record couples entity and table
Cost: extra layer and mapping code
